clue.text: Drive from member landing in poor lie

indicators.note: something landing in a place ends up inside it, so the member's letters go into the reworked lie
a poor lie is a bad one, so its three letters are put in a different order

parts.note: MP stands for Member of Parliament

explanation.surface: A golfer has to play out of a bad lie where the ball has come to rest.
explanation.walkthrough: The golf picture of a drive from a poor lie is the misdirection: 'Drive' is the definition, 'poor' rearranges the lie, and 'landing in' places the member inside it.
explanation.definitionFit: To impel someone is to push or urge them forward, the same as to drive them on.

clue.text: One who stays in, like a monk, with a good book

parts.note: a monk wears a habit, so like a monk is in habit
NT is the New Testament, part of the Bible, the Good Book

explanation.surface: A homebody stays in, quiet as a monk, reading something worthwhile.
explanation.walkthrough: 'stays in' looks like one phrase; split it so 'in' starts the wordplay. A habit is a monk's robe.
explanation.definitionFit: A resident is someone who lives in or occupies a place.

clue.text: Enclosure for a bird

definitions.meaning: a fenced area for animals, such as sheep

explanation.definitionFit: The word means a small fenced pen for livestock and is also the name for a female swan.

clue.text: Instruction given by Trotsky about ship

indicators.note: about here means around, so the name goes round the ship's letters

parts.note: Leon Trotsky was the Russian revolutionary
SS is short for steamship

explanation.surface: A revolutionary lectures on naval matters.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' looks like 'concerning', as if Trotsky lectured on ships, but it is a container signal meaning 'around'.
explanation.definitionFit: A class or teaching session gives instruction to pupils.

clue.text: Persuade to indulge in circumlocution

definitions.meaning: to win someone over to your view by talking
to talk around a subject without ever getting to the point

explanation.definitionFit: Both senses are the same phrasal verb: talking someone round, and talking round a topic.

clue.text: Profuse poet, childless, embraces wife, a senior citizen

indicators.note: to embrace is to hold in one's arms, so the trimmed poet holds the next letters
being childless means having no son, so that word is taken off the poet's name

parts.note: Alfred Tennyson was the Victorian Poet Laureate
OAP is a British old-age pensioner

explanation.surface: A prolific versifier without children hugs his elderly wife.
explanation.walkthrough: 'childless' takes SON off TENNYSON to leave TENNY, which 'embraces' W and OAP (a British old-age pensioner).
explanation.definitionFit: Things so plentiful they would sell two for a penny are abundant and cheap, hence profuse.

clue.text: Joins a course

definitions.meaning: a golf course, especially a seaside one

explanation.definitionFit: The word is a verb for connecting things and a noun for a seaside golf course.

clue.text: Bill, having taken meal outside, after claret, becomes embarrassed

indicators.note: after places the claret's word in front of what follows it here

parts.note: claret is red wine, so it gives red

indicators.note: outside means the word for having eaten goes round the bill

parts.note: someone who has taken a meal has been fed
AC, short for account, is a bill

explanation.surface: After a meal and plenty of red wine, a diner flushes when the bill arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: 'having taken meal' looks like a description of Bill, but it is the outer piece that 'outside' wraps round him; 'after claret' puts the wine's colour first, and 'becomes' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone flushing with shame or awkwardness has gone scarlet in the face.

clue.text: Struck dumb — Helen is flawless

indicators.note: struck suggests a blow that knocks things out of shape, so the next letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone is left speechless by how perfect Helen is.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Struck dumb' reads as one idiom; 'Struck' is the anagram signal and DUMB plus HELEN IS the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: Without a mark or blot, a spotless thing has no flaws at all.

clue.text: Fruit with stone to take out

definitions.meaning: the sweet fruit of a palm, with a single stone
to go out with someone romantically

explanation.definitionFit: The palm fruit has a stone, and taking someone out on a romantic evening is courting them.

clue.text: Passes on with no difficulty at all

definitions.meaning: gives something to a younger generation or a successor

explanation.definitionFit: A hand-me-down is passed on, and an easy win is won without strain, the racing idiom of a jockey not using the whip.

clue.text: Travelled on the Circle Line, returning to where one began

indicators.note: a return trip goes back the other way, so the verb is read from its last letter to its first

parts.note: the Circle Line is part of the London Underground, the Tube, so travelling on it is to have tubed

explanation.surface: A Londoner rides the loop of the Underground and ends up back at the starting station.
explanation.walkthrough: The Circle Line is a London Underground line; to go by Tube is to 'tube', past tense TUBED, and 'returning' turns it round. The circular route makes 'returning to where one began' look like plain description.
explanation.definitionFit: A first appearance, such as an actor's first role, is the point at which a career started.

clue.text: Gapes is bad for exotic migrant

indicators.note: something exotic is strange and foreign, signalling that the preceding words are to be made strange by rearranging

explanation.surface: Someone remarks that staring open-mouthed is a bad thing for a foreign traveller to do.
explanation.walkthrough: All of 'Gapes is bad for' is the fodder, thirteen letters, which 'exotic' rearranges. 'bad' looks like the anagram signal but is part of the fodder.
explanation.definitionFit: A migratory species, or a restless person who moves on, is called this from birds that pass through seasonally.

clue.text: Example of fireworks and larks beginning in love affair

indicators.note: in means these letters are put inside the word for the love affair

parts.note: a romance is a love affair

indicators.note: the beginning of larks is its first letter only

explanation.surface: A passionate affair starts with fireworks and high jinks.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in' is a container signal here, and 'beginning' takes only the first letter of larks. The surface's fireworks are romantic sparks, but the definition means the actual firework.
explanation.definitionFit: This is a firework, a tube that shoots out coloured balls of fire one after another.

clue.text: Noah, for instance, succeeded with it, and with justice

parts.note: S is the abbreviation for succeeded in family trees
with it means fashionable, which is hip
right means justice, as in being in the right

explanation.surface: Noah prospered by being modern and fair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'with it' is one piece (hip) and the second 'with' another (W); 'and' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Noah built the ark, so he is an example of a builder of vessels.

clue.text: Magazine's issue withdrawn

indicators.note: something withdrawn is pulled back, so the verb for issue is read backwards

parts.note: to issue something is to emit or send it out

explanation.surface: A particular edition of a periodical has been pulled from sale.
explanation.walkthrough: The surface suggests a recalled edition; 'issue' is actually a verb, EMIT, and 'withdrawn' turns it back. The 's links definition and wordplay.
explanation.definitionFit: This is the name of a well-known American weekly news periodical.

clue.text: Dines there, given swish food container

indicators.note: a swish movement throws things about, so the letters of the first two words are rearranged

explanation.surface: Someone eats at a smart restaurant and is served from an elegant dish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swish' reads as smart or posh in the surface, but signals rearranging DINES THERE.
explanation.definitionFit: A covered serving vessel for the course before the main meal is a kind of food container.

clue.text: The End of the Affair = book contains new translation

indicators.note: the end of a word is its last letter, here taken from the novel title's final word
contains means the word for book holds the next letter

parts.note: an edition is a printing of a book

explanation.surface: A note says a Graham Greene novel has been freshly translated.
explanation.walkthrough: The italics invite reading the Graham Greene title as one unit; 'End of' takes R from 'the Affair', and 'contains' puts N inside EDITION.
explanation.definitionFit: A rendering of a text in another language, or a performance of a song, is a version or translation.

clue.text: You can see it run along rope and quickly put on speed

definitions.text: You can see it run along rope

parts.note: to slip something on is to put it on quickly, like a coat
a knot is a unit of speed at sea

explanation.surface: A sailor watches a line racing along and the boat picking up pace.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put on speed' reads as accelerating, but splits into 'quickly put on' and 'speed'. 'and' links.
explanation.definitionFit: This kind of knot is tied so that it slides along the rope it is made on.

clue.text: Sort of captain sporting a long pinny

indicators.note: sporting can mean playing about, so these letters are played with and rearranged

explanation.surface: A team leader turns up wearing an oversized apron.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sporting' looks like 'wearing' but rearranges A LONG PINNY (a pinny is a British word for a pinafore apron).
explanation.definitionFit: A team skipper who selects and leads but does not take the field, as in Davis Cup tennis, is this sort of captain.

clue.text: Fish caught by chance, once

parts.note: C is the cricket abbreviation for caught
hap is an old word for luck or chance, the once marking it as archaic

explanation.surface: An angler lands a fish purely by luck.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish' looks like a creature but means a person, as in 'a queer fish'; 'by' links the pieces in the charade.
explanation.definitionFit: A person can be called an odd fish, so fish is a jocular word for a fellow.

clue.text: Businessman, in parts, is convincing

parts.note: the word's first part, business, is a company, CO
the word's second part, man, is a gentleman, GENT

explanation.surface: A salesman makes a persuasive pitch, bit by bit.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in parts' tells you to split the single word 'Businessman' into its two halves and find a short synonym for each; 'is' links.
explanation.definitionFit: A strong, persuasive argument is said to be compelling or forceful.

clue.text: Request for sweet in perfect condition

parts.note: a sweet is a pudding, and apple pie is one
an order is a request for something, as in a restaurant

explanation.surface: A diner asks for a pudding that arrives looking immaculate.
explanation.walkthrough: Ordering an apple pie, read with the words swapped round, gives the phrase; 'in' is the link to the definition. British 'sweet' means dessert.
explanation.definitionFit: Something arranged neatly and tidily, everything in its place, is in this state of order.

clue.text: Whole-hearted boost for halfhearted music

indicators.note: to boost is to push up, and in a down answer pushing letters up reads them backwards
the heart of the music word is its doubled middle pair, and losing half of it drops one letter

parts.note: reggae is Jamaican music

explanation.surface: Enthusiastic encouragement for music played without much feeling.
explanation.walkthrough: 'halfhearted' cuts one G from REGGAE's middle GG to give REGAE, and 'boost' lifts it, reading upwards to give the answer. 'for' links.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone keen and enthusiastic throws themselves into something with all their heart.

clue.text: Errant husband's caught in this way

indicators.note: the letters of the answer are caught in the clue's first two words, spanning them

explanation.surface: A straying husband is caught in the act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Errant' looks like an anagram signal, but the answer runs across the end of 'Errant' and the start of 'husband's'.
explanation.definitionFit: The adverb means in this manner, or so.

clue.text: Worn and ragged

definitions.meaning: was wearing, as in having had a coat on
teased or made fun of someone, playing a trick on them

explanation.definitionFit: Clothes someone wore were the things they had on, and to tease or fool someone is to have them on.

clue.text: Subject of experiment 252d — lump of metal

parts.note: 252 old pence is 21 shillings, the old British coin and sum called a guinea
a pig is an oblong mass of cast metal, as in pig iron

explanation.surface: A lab report lists a cost in old money and a chunk of iron.
explanation.walkthrough: Before 1971 British money had pence (d) and shillings; 252d is 21 shillings, a guinea. A pig is an ingot of smelted metal.
explanation.definitionFit: Small rodents were long used in laboratory tests, so the name now means anyone experimented on.

clue.text: Dog, a boxer

definitions.meaning: short for pugilist, a fighter with fists

explanation.definitionFit: The breed is a small snub-nosed dog, and the word is also slang for a prizefighter.

clue.text: Is there no alloy in this metal?

indicators.note: an alloy is a blend of metals, so the letters of the first three words are blended together

explanation.surface: A puzzled metallurgist asks whether a sample is pure rather than mixed.
explanation.walkthrough: 'alloy' sounds like part of the question but mixes IS THERE NO; 'in this' links to the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Iron rolled into thin flat plates is a form of the metal used in building and roofing.

clue.text: Drunk reluctant to part with money

explanation.definitionFit: The word is informal both for being intoxicated and for being stingy.
